cards.text: This song comes from the sons of Korah, a family of Levite singers (2 Chr 20:19), and they're talking straight to God. They start with what their fathers told them: the work God did in their days, in the days of old. My boy Chip begged me for one more story every night, and I promise you none of mine were THIS good.

cards.question: In those old stories their fathers told, what did God do to the nations living in the land?

answers.text: Drove them out with His hand
Made them friends of their fathers
Let them share the land in peace

cards.question: The singers say their fathers took the land by their own sword and the strength of their own arm.

cards.text: Not their sword, not their arm: it was God's right hand, His arm and the light of His face. Their fathers got that land the way I'd get a perfect batch handed to me while I'm still looking for the mixing bowl.

cards.question: The song says God gave their fathers the land. Why did He do it?

cards.text: Then the psalmist moves from the past to right now: "You are my King, O God, who ordains victories for Jacob." Jacob was Israel's forefather (Gen 32:28), and here his name means his whole people.

cards.question: Now they've got enemies of their own. What does the psalmist say he's counting on to win?

cards.text: He says it straight out: he doesn't trust in his bow, and his sword doesn't save him.

God saves them from their enemies and puts those who hate them to shame, and they say, "In God we have boasted all day long, and Your name we will praise forever." Not a little brag here and there, friend, but ALL DAY LONG.

cards.question: Up to this point in Psalm 44, what's the mood of the song?

cards.text: Everything's going great. Then one little word flips the whole song: "But You have rejected and humbled us; You no longer go forth with our armies."

cards.question: With God no longer going out with their armies, the singers say they still beat every foe.

cards.text: They retreat from the foe, and those who hate them plunder them. They say God has given them up as sheep to be devoured and scattered them among the nations.

cards.question: The singers say God sells His people for ___.

cards.text: He sells His people for nothing and gains no profit from the sale. Friend, I got sold for 25 cents out of a bakery's clearance bin, and I thought THAT was a low price tag.

cards.question: The singers say the nations around them treat them with respect.
Earlier, the singers boasted in God all day long. Now the psalmist says that all day long, his ___ is before him.

cards.text: They're a byword among the nations and a laughingstock, and shame covers his face at the voice of the scorner and the reviler, the enemy bent on revenge. This song went from a victory parade to rock bottom in eight verses.
The psalmist looks at all of it, the retreat, the plunder, the mockery, and says all this has come upon them. So here's the big question: did they bring it on themselves?

cards.question: The psalmist says all this happened because they forgot God and betrayed His covenant.

cards.text: Their hearts have not turned back, and their steps have not strayed from God's path. These folks are holding on.

cards.question: Even so, the psalmist says God has crushed them in the lair of jackals and covered them with ___.
The psalmist says that if they had forgotten God's name or spread out their hands to a foreign god, God would have discovered it.

cards.text: God knows the secrets of the heart, so nobody's sneaking anything past Him. Friend, I can't even sneak one cookie off the cooling rack without the crumbs in my mustache snitching on me.

cards.question: The psalmist says they face death all day long. For whose sake?

cards.text: And here come the sheep again: they're considered as sheep to be slaughtered. The apostle Paul quotes this line in Romans 8:36, right in the middle of asking who can separate us from the love of Christ (Rom 8:35).

cards.question: The psalmist has stayed faithful, and he's still crushed. What does he cry out to God?

cards.text: Then the psalmist cries out, "Wake up, O Lord! Why are You sleeping? Arise! Do not reject us forever." I think that's a man who still believes God can answer, or he wouldn't bother asking.

cards.question: The psalmist asks God why He hides His face.

cards.text: He asks why God forgets their affliction and oppression. Friend, I spent years in the back of a junk drawer, so I know how heavy that word forget can feel.

cards.question: The psalmist says their soul has sunk to the ___ and their bodies cling to the earth.
Down in the dust, the psalmist asks God to rise up and redeem them. On account of what?

cards.text: "Rise up; be our help! Redeem us on account of Your loving devotion." And the song ends right there, still calling out to God.

findings.problem: Nothing in the earlier cards lets the baker reason whether God sells His people for nothing, silver or gold. The blank therefore asks for wording the baker has not seen and can only guess, rather than testing a meaning they can work out.

rule.text: The blank tests meaning the baker can reason out, not wording they haven't seen.

findings.problem: The card retells the retreat and plunder from verse 10 and the mockery from verses 13-16, but cites only Psalm 44:17. Its citation needs to span the earlier material it uses through verse 17, rather than covering only the newest verse.

rule.text: Every story card cites the verses it tells, from the first verse it uses to the last, no wider and no narrower.
